title: Hierarchical ODE: Learning Continuous-Time Physical Prototypes
one_liner: Instead of using a discrete model to find the underlying patterns in a noisy time series, the paper uses a continuous mathematical model that learns steady trends separately from random noise.
lead: When you watch a network of cables over time, you see jittering measurements mixed with real shifts in the underlying state. Discrete models (which work on individual time steps) cannot pull these apart. This paper learns a continuous model instead, one that evolves smoothly through time, so it naturally separates the real trends from the random wobbles. It also figures out how many distinct failure patterns exist instead of guessing.

problem.h2: Two problems with time series clustering
paras: Suppose you measure a network link every second for an hour, and some measurements jump around randomly. You want to know: what are the two or three truly different states this link lives in? One approach is to look at each time step independently, cluster the measurements into groups, and call those groups the prototypes. But this fails: random noise gets treated as evidence of a new pattern.
Second problem: you do not know in advance how many clusters should exist. Discrete models need you to guess the number, and if you guess wrong, you either miss patterns or invent fake ones.

callout.html: Instead of clustering the raw measurements at each instant, learn a smooth model that evolves over time and simultaneously figures out the right number of clusters.

steps.text: Take an irregularly sampled time series (cable link measurements).
A neural ODE tracks the underlying state: pretend it flows like water following an invisible current.
During training, the model learns which latent states are stable (prototypes) and which are just noise.
A hierarchical mechanism activates only the prototypes needed; extra capacity remains zero.
If a new measurement drifts toward the critical-failure prototype, raise an alarm.

paras: Instead of clustering individual noisy measurements, the paper changes the hidden state model itself. It swaps a discrete step-by-step model for a continuous trajectory model (a neural ODE, which is a mathematical system that describes how things change over time). This single choice forces the model to separate smooth trends from random jitter automatically.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: stable attractor points
hidden.name: attractor strength
paras: Every time series has underlying stable states where the system naturally sits. A cable network might have a normal-operation state, a mild-degradation state, and a critical-failure state. These are called attractor points: the system is pulled toward them.

The paper measures how strong each attractor is: how much does the continuous model converge toward that point over time? A strong attractor means the system reliably settles into that state. Weak attractors are noise artifacts. The hierarchical mechanism counts only the strong ones, ignoring the fake ones invented by random noise.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger attractor. Weak attractors (noise artifacts) are ignored; strong ones become prototypes.

reads.html: An attractor is a state the system returns to, like water draining downhill toward a valley. A strong attractor is a deep valley; a weak one is a shallow puddle.
The paper learns latent trajectories via neural ODE and measures the convergence rate and long-term behavior to identify stable equilibrium points as prototypes.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: continuous models decouple signal from noise
paras: A discrete model (one that makes a decision at each time step) sees every jitter as a potential cluster member. Random noise looks identical to a real trend. A continuous model behaves differently: it evolves along a smooth path, integrating all the measurements into a flowing trajectory. Random noise pulls the trajectory sideways momentarily, but the integration smooths it out. The model learns that noise is a tiny, temporary bump; true patterns are large, persistent trends.

The second key: a hierarchical mechanism. Instead of guessing how many clusters exist upfront, the model activates cluster units on demand. If the data does not need a fifth cluster, the fifth unit stays off. This adaptive counting works because during training, the loss penalizes the model if it activates a cluster unit that the data does not actually need—unused units contribute no reconstruction signal and waste model capacity—so the model learns to leave unused units off and activate only prototypes that explain the measurements.

stages.s: Neural ODE integrator traces latent trajectory
Reconstruction compares model trajectory to real data
Hierarchical prototype selector identifies stable points
Predicted cluster labels and failure risk

math.words: The latent state evolves as the integral of its derivative, where the derivative is learned by a neural network.
math.equation: z(t) = z(t0) + integral from t0 to t of f_theta(z(s)) ds
symbols: the hidden state at time t
a tiny time step in the integral

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: At time t=0.0 to t=0.1: derivative f(0.5) = -0.1 (drifting slightly downward).
At t=0.1 to t=0.2: derivative f(0.49) = -0.08 (weaker pull, approaching stable point).
The state converges smoothly toward equilibrium z* = 0.0 (the attractor). Random noise at any step perturbs the state briefly but the ODE's smoothness recovers.

math.note: The integral enforces continuity: the latent path is a smooth curve, never a jagged jump. Noise causes small detours, but the underlying drift back to stable points defines the true prototypes.

charts.title: Discrete clustering (naive method)
charts.note: Discrete models cluster at each time step independently, confusing noise with real patterns. They find many spurious clusters and miss some true states.

charts.title: Hierarchical ODE (this paper)
charts.note: Continuous model with adaptive hierarchy separates noise from signal and learns only real prototypes, achieving clean detection across all states.

items.html: If the underlying system has true jumps (e.g., a relay that switches instantly), a continuous ODE model will try to smooth them and miss the sharp transition. The paper assumes underlying continuous dynamics.
If the hierarchical selector is too deep, it can activate unnecessary prototypes, especially if the data is noisy. The model needs tuning to balance expressiveness with parsimony.
If measurements are so sparse that hours pass between samples, the ODE integrator has to extrapolate over a long gap, and errors accumulate. Very sparse data breaks the continuous assumption.

When data is fundamentally continuous (physical processes, link metrics, sensor streams) and measurements are reasonably dense, the ODE model naturally learns clean prototypes and scales to the number of distinct failure modes.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic time series with three stable states (normal, mild, critical) plus realistic noise. Train a discrete k-means model and the hierarchical ODE model. Measure: (1) do both models correctly identify the three prototypes? (2) does the ODE use exactly three cluster units while k-means needs many more? (3) when you simulate a new trajectory drifting from normal to critical, does only the ODE's early warning activate smoothly?
demo.closing: The demo's payoff: the ODE model gives smooth, interpretable warnings with no spurious cluster assignments, while discrete clustering floods you with false alarms.
